paragraphs: The word “poetry” has been given several different meanings. It would weary my readers if I led them into a discussion of which of these definitions should be chosen. I prefer to tell them at once which one I have chosen. In my opinion, poetry is the search for and the portrayal of the ideal. The poet is the one who completes and extends the work of nature. He does so by suppressing part of what exists, by adding some imaginary touches to the picture, and by combining certain real circumstances that do not in fact occur together. Thus the object of poetry is not to represent what is true, but to adorn it and to present to the mind some loftier imagery. Verse, regarded as the ideal beauty of language, may be eminently poetic, but verse by itself does not constitute poetry.

I now go on to ask whether, among the actions, feelings, and opinions of democratic nations, there are any that lead to a conception of ideal beauty, and that may for this reason be considered natural sources of poetry. We must first acknowledge that the taste for ideal beauty, and the pleasure of expressing it, are never so intense or so widespread among a democratic people as among an aristocratic one. In aristocratic nations it sometimes happens that the body goes on acting, as it were, spontaneously, while the higher faculties are bound and weighed down by repose. Among these nations the people very often show poetic tastes, and sometimes let their fancy range beyond and above what surrounds them. But in democracies the love of physical gratification, the idea of bettering one’s condition, the excitement of rivalry, and the charm of anticipated success are so many spurs driving men forward in the active professions they have taken up, without letting them stray from the track for an instant. The main stress of the faculties is directed to this point. The imagination is not extinct, but its chief function is to devise what may be useful and to represent what is real.

The principle of equality not only turns men away from portraying ideal beauty; it also reduces the number of objects to be portrayed. Aristocracy holds society in a fixed position. This favors the solidity and duration of positive religions, as well as the stability of political institutions. It not only keeps the human mind within a certain sphere of belief, but also predisposes it to adopt one faith rather than another. An aristocratic people will always be inclined to place intermediate powers between God and man. In this respect it may be said that the aristocratic element is favorable to poetry. When the universe is peopled with supernatural creatures, not perceptible to the senses but discovered by the mind, the imagination ranges freely. Poets then find a thousand subjects to portray, and they also find a countless audience interested in their works. In democratic ages, on the contrary, it sometimes happens that men are as adrift in matters of belief as they are in their laws. Skepticism then draws the poets’ imagination back to earth and confines them to the real and visible world. Even when the principle of equality does not disturb religious belief, it tends to simplify it, and to turn attention away from secondary agents and fix it chiefly on the Supreme Power. Aristocracy naturally leads the human mind to contemplate the past and holds it there. Democracy, on the contrary, gives men a kind of instinctive distaste for what is ancient. In this respect aristocracy is far more favorable to poetry, for things commonly grow larger and more obscure the more remote they are. For this twofold reason they are better suited to the portrayal of the ideal.

Having deprived poetry of the past, the principle of equality robs it in part of the present. Among aristocratic nations there are a certain number of privileged persons whose situation is, as it were, outside and above the condition of man. Power, wealth, fame, wit, refinement, and distinction in all things appear to belong especially to them. The crowd never sees them very closely, or does not watch them in minute detail, and little is needed to make the description of such men poetic. On the other hand, among the same people you will find classes so ignorant, low, and enslaved that they are no less fit objects for poetry, because of the extremity of their rudeness and wretchedness, than the former are because of their greatness and refinement. Besides, the different classes that make up an aristocratic community are widely separated and imperfectly acquainted with each other. The imagination can therefore always represent them with something added to, or subtracted from, what they really are. In democratic communities, where men are all insignificant and very much alike, each man sees all his fellows the moment he looks at himself. The poets of democratic ages can therefore never take any one man as the subject of a piece. An object of slight importance, seen distinctly on all sides, will never lend itself to an ideal conception. Thus, as the principle of equality has established itself in the world, it has dried up most of the old springs of poetry. Let us now try to show what new ones it may open.

Skepticism had emptied heaven, and the progress of equality had reduced each individual to smaller and better known proportions. The poets did not yet know what they could put in place of the great themes that were departing along with the aristocracy, so they turned their eyes to inanimate nature. As they lost sight of gods and heroes, they set themselves to describe streams and mountains. This is the origin, in the last century, of the kind of poetry that has been called, by way of distinction, descriptive. Some have thought that this sort of portrayal, embellished with all the physical and inanimate objects that cover the earth, was the kind of poetry peculiar to democratic ages. But I believe this is a mistake, and that it belongs only to a period of transition.

I am convinced that in the end democracy turns the imagination away from everything external to man and fixes it on man alone. Democratic nations may amuse themselves for a while by considering the productions of nature, but they are truly excited only by a survey of themselves. Here, and here alone, are the true sources of poetry among such nations to be found. It may be believed that poets who neglect to draw their inspiration from this source will lose all sway over the minds they want to enchant, and will be left in the end with none but unmoved spectators of their raptures. I have shown how the ideas of progress and of the indefinite perfectibility of the human race belong to democratic ages. Democratic nations care little for what has been, but they are haunted by visions of what will be. In this direction their unbounded imagination grows and expands beyond all measure. Here, then, is the wildest range open to the genius of poets, which lets them place their works at a sufficient distance from the eye. Democracy shuts the past against the poet, but opens the future before him. All the citizens who make up a democratic community are nearly equal and alike, so the poet cannot dwell on any one of them. But the nation itself invites the exercise of his powers. The general similarity of individuals makes any one of them, taken separately, an improper subject of poetry. Yet it allows poets to include them all in the same imagery and to take a general survey of the people itself. Democratic nations have a clearer perception than any others of their own aspect, and an aspect so imposing is admirably suited to the portrayal of the ideal.

I readily admit that the Americans have no poets, but I cannot allow that they have no poetic ideas. In Europe people talk a great deal about the wilds of America, but the Americans themselves never think about them. They are insensible to the wonders of inanimate nature, and it may be said that they do not notice the mighty forests that surround them until they fall beneath the hatchet. Their eyes are fixed on another sight. The American people sees itself marching across these wilds, draining swamps, turning the course of rivers, peopling solitudes, and subduing nature. This magnificent image of themselves does not meet the gaze of the Americans only at intervals. It may be said to haunt every one of them in his smallest as well as his most important actions, and to be always flitting before his mind. Nothing imaginable is so petty, so insipid, so crowded with paltry interests — in a word, so anti-poetic — as the life of a man in the United States. But among the thoughts it suggests there is always one full of poetry, and that is the hidden nerve that gives vigor to the whole frame.

In aristocratic ages each people, like each individual, tends to stand separate and aloof from all others. In democratic ages, the extreme restlessness of men and the impatience of their desires keep them perpetually on the move. The inhabitants of different countries therefore mingle, and they see, listen to, and borrow from each other’s stores. It is not only the members of the same community who grow more alike. Communities themselves become assimilated to one another, and the whole assemblage presents to the eye of the spectator one vast democracy, each citizen of which is a people. This shows the aspect of mankind in the broadest light for the first time. All that belongs to the existence of the human race taken as a whole, to its changes of fortune and to its future, becomes an abundant mine of poetry. The poets who lived in aristocratic ages were eminently successful in portraying certain incidents in the life of a people or a man. But none of them ever ventured to include the destinies of mankind in his works, a task that poets writing in democratic ages may attempt. At the same time that every man, raising his eyes above his country, begins at last to see mankind at large, the Divinity becomes more and more visible to the human mind in full and entire majesty. In democratic ages, faith in positive religions is often shaken, and belief in intermediate agents, by whatever name they are called, is clouded. On the other hand, men are inclined to form a far broader idea of Providence itself, and its interference in human affairs takes on a new and more imposing appearance in their eyes. Looking at the human race as one great whole, they easily conceive that its destinies are governed by a single design. In the actions of every individual they are led to recognize a trace of that universal and eternal plan by which God rules our race. This consideration may be taken as another rich source of poetry opened in democratic ages. Democratic poets will always appear trivial and frigid if they try to give gods, demons, or angels bodily forms, or if they attempt to draw them down from heaven to dispute the supremacy of earth. But suppose they strive to connect the great events they commemorate with the general providential designs that govern the universe, and, without showing the finger of the Supreme Governor, reveal the thoughts of the Supreme Mind. Then their works will be admired and understood, for the imagination of their contemporaries takes this direction of its own accord.

In the same way, it may be foreseen that poets living in democratic ages will prefer portraying passions and ideas to portraying persons and achievements. The language, the dress, and the daily actions of men in democracies are repugnant to ideal conceptions. These things are not poetic in themselves. And if it were otherwise, they would cease to be poetic, because they are too familiar to all those to whom the poet would speak of them. This forces the poet constantly to search below the external surface that the senses can perceive, in order to read the inner soul. Nothing lends itself more to the portrayal of the ideal than the scrutiny of the hidden depths in the immaterial nature of man. I do not need to wander over earth and sky to discover a wondrous object woven of contrasts, of infinite greatness and littleness, of intense gloom and amazing brightness, capable at once of exciting pity, admiration, terror, and contempt. I find that object in myself. Man springs out of nothing, crosses time, and disappears forever in the bosom of God. He is seen only for a moment, staggering on the verge of the two abysses, and there he is lost. If man were wholly ignorant of himself, he would have no poetry in him, for it is impossible to describe what the mind does not conceive. If man clearly saw his own nature, his imagination would remain idle and would have nothing to add to the picture. But the nature of man is disclosed enough for him to grasp something of himself, and obscure enough for all the rest to be plunged in thick darkness, in which he gropes forever, and forever in vain, to lay hold of some fuller notion of his being.

Among a democratic people, poetry will not be fed on legendary lays or the memorials of old traditions. The poet will not attempt to people the universe with supernatural beings in whom his readers and his own fancy have ceased to believe. Nor will he present virtues and vices in the mask of frigid personification, when they are better received under their own features. All these resources fail him, but Man remains, and the poet needs no more. The destinies of mankind will become the chief theme of poetry among these nations, if not the only one. By this I mean man himself, taken apart from his age and his country, standing in the presence of Nature and of God, with his passions, his doubts, his rare prosperities, and his inconceivable wretchedness. Experience may confirm this assertion if we consider the works of the greatest poets who have appeared since the world turned to democracy. The authors of our age who have so admirably portrayed the features of Faust, Childe Harold, Rene, and Jocelyn did not seek to record the actions of an individual. They sought to enlarge and to throw light on some of the obscurer recesses of the human heart. Such are the poems of democracy. The principle of equality, then, does not destroy all the subjects of poetry. It makes them fewer, but more vast.
